title: Cool versus warm water for facial cleansing: a 10-day barrier trial
headline: Ten days of warm-water face washing raised water loss through the skin (about 3.4 g/m2/h) while cool water did not, with the same make-up removal, in a 52-person industry-linked trial. It is free to try, but it is one small study read at abstract level only.
evidenceTier: Single randomized controlled study, 10 days, 52 adults. Abstract read; full text not opened (no free full text found)
fit: Strong on barrier as a zero-cost, reversible change. The abstract says nothing about skin tone, oily or breakout-prone skin, or retinoid-treated skin, and does not define warm and cool in degrees.
displaces: Nothing. It changes the water temperature of an existing cleansing step.
buzzCheck: Nothing to buy, so no buzz premium. The sustainability framing is the sponsor's; the barrier result is the part that matters for skin.
summaryPoints: Design (abstract): 10-day randomized study, 52 healthy adults (46 women, 6 men, aged 19-72) cleansed daily with the same cleansing balm under four conditions: cool or warm water, tap off during cleansing or left running.

Reported: warm water produced a significant rise in water loss through the skin (TEWL, about +3.4 g/m2/h at day 10, p<0.01); cool water produced no significant change (about +1, p=0.15). Surface pH fell by about 0.4 with cool water (p<0.02). Make-up removal did not differ by temperature. Warm cleansing used about 27% more water.
Skin hydration fell modestly in all groups, so cool water did not improve hydration.

Caveats: authors are from the cleansing-balm brand and a contract research firm; the abstract gives no temperatures, no skin-tone data and no adverse-event information; I could not open the full text.
fitLine: Low-risk barrier change with a measured instrument effect; evidence is small and sponsor-linked.
timeline: Water-loss divergence measured by day 10; felt change unknown

fitAxes.why: The one measured effect was protection of barrier function (water loss) over 10 days versus warm water.
Not tested on retinoid-treated skin. Retinoids tend to raise water loss, so a gentler wash is plausibly helpful (my inference).
Not assessed. With oil-based or sunscreen-heavy routines, cool water may emulsify less well (my inference); the trial's make-up test used a balm.
Likely easiest in warm months; in cold, dry months the barrier argument is stronger but cool water is less comfortable.

dossier.whatItIs: A behavioural change, not a product: wash the face with cool rather than warm water. The study asks whether water temperature matters for the skin barrier and for removing make-up, and what it does to water and energy use.

steps: The abstract reports outcomes only: water loss through the skin (TEWL), skin hydration, surface pH, radiance and make-up removal.
Warm-water cleansing increased TEWL over 10 days; cool water did not.
No mechanism is given in the abstract. The usual explanation is that heat strips surface lipids and loosens the outer layer, but this study did not test that.
mechanism.inferenceFlag: The lipid-stripping explanation is my inference from general skin physiology, not something the abstract shows.
mechanism.diagramCaption: Warm water daily -> higher water loss by day 10; cool water daily -> no significant change

flow.label: Warm or cool water with a cleansing balm, daily
flow.note: Four groups; temperatures not given in the abstract.

flow.label: Barrier function measured by TEWL over 10 days
flow.note: Warm: about +3.4 g/m2/h at day 10 (p<0.01). Cool: not significant.

studies.cite: Long S, Fenn K, Harvey K, Ward P, O'Brien C. Cool versus warm water for facial cleansing: A randomized controlled clinical study of skin barrier, skin physiology, cleansing efficacy and water consumption. Int J Cosmet Sci. 2026 Sep 10.
studies.readDepth: Abstract only (no open full text found; full text not opened)
studies.design: 10-day randomized controlled study; 52 healthy adults (46 women, 6 men, 19-72 years); four arms (cool or warm water, tap off or running) using one cleansing balm daily. TEWL (Tewameter), hydration (Corneometer), pH, radiance and make-up removal (colourimetric) at baseline and days 1, 2, 4, 7, 10. Water use covertly metered.
studies.who: Healthy adults. Skin type, tone and baseline barrier status are not reported in the abstract.
results: Warm water: TEWL up about 3.4 g/m2/h at day 10 (p<0.01).
Cool water: TEWL change about 1 g/m2/h (p=0.15, not significant).
Cool water: surface pH fell about 0.4 (p<0.02); no change with warm.
Hydration declined modestly in all groups.
Make-up removal did not differ between temperatures (p>0.05); warm used about 27% more water (p<0.04).
studies.effectSize: Differences in TEWL and pH given above; group sizes per arm are not in the abstract (about 13 per arm if evenly split, my arithmetic).
studies.placebo: No inactive arm. The comparison is cool versus warm water.
studies.material: Not established. A 3.4 g/m2/h change in water loss is a modest instrument change, and whether it is felt is unknown.
studies.conflict: Authors are from Elemis Ltd (the maker of the cleansing balm used) and Cutest Systems Ltd (a contract research organisation).
studies.limits: Short (10 days), about a dozen people per arm if evenly split, sponsor-linked, one cleanser, no skin-tone or skin-type breakdown in the abstract, temperatures unspecified. Single study; no replication found.

claimsCheck.claim: Cool-water cleansing preserves the skin barrier and matches warm water for make-up removal
claimsCheck.status: Supported by the abstract's numbers for a balm and make-up; not tested for sunscreen, oil cleansers or other skin types

products.rankNote: No product involved. The study used a branded cleansing balm; no product recommendation follows from it.

howToUse: Swap lukewarm or warm rinse water for cool: noticeably below skin temperature, not icy. The abstract gives no temperatures, so this is my reading of 'cool'.
Try it for 10 days, matching the trial. Watch for tightness, flaking or leftover residue.
If you use oil cleansers or heavy sunscreens, check that cool water still rinses them off well; the trial's make-up test used a balm and may not transfer.
Do not add new steps. The point is to change one variable.

expect.what: Little to feel. Water-loss differences in the trial emerged slowly.
The point at which warm-water TEWL was clearly higher in the trial.

dossier.contraindications: No harms reported in the abstract. Cold-triggered conditions are the obvious exception (my inference). Not tested in skin disease.
dossier.sideBenefits: About 27% less water used per cleanse (trial figure).
wouldChangeVerdict: Independent replication, ideally 4 weeks or more
Results in deeper skin tones, oily and acne-prone skin, and retinoid users
Full text showing the actual temperatures and per-arm numbers
Data with oil cleansers and sunscreen removal
dossier.transfer: Skin tone is not reported. Heat and surface lipids are not skin-tone specific as far as I know, so the barrier effect plausibly applies by mechanism, but that is my inference; the study cannot confirm it.
confidence: Abstract only. Not opened: full text (no free version found).
Not verified: per-arm numbers, actual temperatures, adverse events, funding statement.
